clean_source_blocks.text: The BBC asked Americans how they felt after the Supreme Court's ruling on citizenship for babies born in the US.

Oklahoma leaders are reacting to the Supreme Court’s decision to uphold birthright citizenship, rejecting President Donald Trump’s executive order, which sought to deny automatic American citizenship to babies born to parents in the country illegally or temporarily. Related Story: Supreme Court upholds birthright citizenship, striking down Trump’s order Oklahoma’s Own Political Analyst Scott Mitchell said the ruling is a case of limits vs control. “The president put an executive order out, no birthright citizenship, it’s gone. And the states that challenged that, they won. And I’m sure that the president, the administration, is seething over this. But it’s limits versus control. Are we going to give him more control over the executive? Yes. Are we going to take away limits, let him override the Constitution? The Supreme Court said no,” said Mitchell.

The Supreme Court has ruled that babies born in the US have a constitutional right to citizenship, rejecting Donald Trump's bid to end the 150-year-old policy. In a 6-3 decision, Chief Justice John Roberts ruled that children born in the US "to parents unlawfully or temporarily present" are "citizens at birth" under the 14th Amendment. Trump had sought to limit the right through an executive order. Read more about the ruling that many say is a major setback for President Trump's immigration agenda. ---

The Supreme Court on June 30 rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to limit birthright citizenship in a move Massachusetts politicians applauded. "Today's decision upholds a fundamental constitutional principle that has defined our nation for generations,” Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. “Birthright citizenship is central to who we are as a nation. It has provided certainty for families across the country and protects the rights of children born on American soil. The Supreme Court made clear today: President Trump can’t rewrite the Constitution.” In the 6-3 ruling, the justices said Trump cannot change the definition of birthright citizenship with the stroke of a pen. Trump's push to make that change upended how the constitutional guarantee – long considered a bedrock American principle — had historically been understood.

[Lähde: BBC World]
The Supreme Court has ruled that babies born in the US have a constitutional right to citizenship, rejecting Donald Trump's bid to end the 150-year-old policy. In a 6-3 decision, Chief Justice John Roberts ruled that children born in the US "to parents unlawfully or temporarily present" are "citizens at birth" under the 14th Amendment. Trump had sought to limit the right through an executive order.

---

[Lähde: News 9]
Oklahoma leaders are reacting to the Supreme Court’s decision to uphold birthright citizenship, rejecting President Donald Trump’s executive order, which sought to deny automatic American citizenship to babies born to parents in the country illegally or temporarily.

Related Story: Supreme Court upholds birthright citizenship, striking down Trump’s order

Oklahoma’s Own Political Analyst Scott Mitchell said the ruling is a case of limits vs control.

“The president put an executive order out, no birthright citizenship, it’s gone. And the states that challenged that, they won. And I’m sure that the president, the administration, is seething over this. But it’s limits versus control. Are we going to give him more control over the executive? Yes. Are we going to take away limits, let him override the Constitution? The Supreme Court said no,” said Mitchell.

The Supreme Court also ruled states can prohibit transgender athletes from competing on girls’ and women’s sports teams, a decision that delivers the latest setback for transgender rights. Mitchell called the ruling fairly narrow, as it only addresses sports and athletics, leaving the larger conversations around transgender rights still undecided.

“It probably eliminates this mismatch, this quilt of various laws all around the country. The Supreme Court has ruled only in athletic cases that the bans do not violate Title IX, and they do not violate the Equal Justice Clause of the 14th Amendment. So for now, unless it moves to the federal Congress, it’s probably shut the door. Justice Sotomayor has objected and said the bigger rights issue still is out there to be dealt with. But for athletics, this probably takes away a lot of the campaign commercials we’ve been seeing over the last year. It settles it, at least in the athletic field. If you think this is going to stop the broader culture war arena or theater. I don’t think that a person would have a handle on reality,” said Mitchell

Related Story: Supreme Court upholds state bans on transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports

Gov. Kevin Stitt joined News 9 and said that the Supreme Court got it wrong regarding birthright citizenship because other countries don’t do it that way.

“That’s one that, when you really stop and think about it, most other countries, and Trump’s pointed this out several times, they protect their citizenship. So, all Trump was trying to ask the question, which I totally agree with him. I think the Supreme Court got it wrong

---

[Lähde: USA TODAY]
The Supreme Court on June 30 rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to limit birthright citizenship in a move Massachusetts politicians applauded.

"Today's decision upholds a fundamental constitutional principle that has defined our nation for generations,” Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. “Birthright citizenship is central to who we are as a nation. It has provided certainty for families across the country and protects the rights of children born on American soil.  The Supreme Court made clear today: President Trump can’t rewrite the Constitution.”

In the 6-3 ruling, the justices said Trump cannot change the definition of birthright citizenship with the stroke of a pen. Trump's push to make that change upended how the constitutional guarantee – long considered a bedrock American principle — had historically been understood.

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the opinion. Three of the court's other conservatives dissented.

Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell, one of the 22 attorneys general that sued Trump over his initial executive order, said that if it wasn’t for the Fourteenth Amendment, which has served as the basis for birthright citizenship, she could not have run to become attorney general.

“For more than 150 years, the Fourteenth Amendment has stood as a cornerstone of equal protection under the law, born out of our nation’s fight to end slavery and oppression,” Campbell said in a statement. "Today, the Supreme Court left in place the principle that the President cannot rewrite the Constitution by executive order, and birthright citizenship remains settled law.”

The ruling came months after the court killed Trump’s signature tariffs, another repudiation of the expansive authority Trump has claimed since returning to the White House last year.

But in other immigration cases, including last week’s ruling allowing Trump to end deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of immigrants, the justices backed the president’s authority.

Campbell and Massachusetts’s two senators, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Ed Markey, D-Mass., emphasized that this case is not the end. Campbell called it a “razor thin victory,” and Markey said the “fight is far from over.”

“The fight to defend immigrant rights from Trump's cruelty is not over, but today the Court upheld the law,” Warren said in a statement on social media. “It's simple: if you're born in America, you're an American.”

payload.title: Yhdysvaltain korkein oikeus torjui Trumpin yrityksen rajata syntymäoikeuteen perustuvaa kansalaisuutta
payload.summary: Yhdysvaltain korkein oikeus katsoi äänin 6–3, että maassa syntyneillä lapsilla on perustuslaillinen oikeus kansalaisuuteen myös silloin, kun heidän vanhempansa ovat maassa laittomasti tai väliaikaisesti.
payload.content:
Yhdysvaltain korkein oikeus on torjunut presidentti Donald Trumpin yrityksen rajata syntymäoikeuteen perustuvaa kansalaisuutta. Ratkaisun mukaan Yhdysvalloissa syntyneet lapset ovat kansalaisia syntymästään lähtien myös silloin, kun heidän vanhempansa ovat maassa laittomasti tai väliaikaisesti.

## Päätös pysäytti presidentin määräyksen

Ratkaisu annettiin äänin 6–3. Päätuomari John Robertsin mukaan Yhdysvalloissa syntyneet lapset, joiden vanhemmat ovat maassa ilman laillista oleskeluoikeutta tai tilapäisesti, ovat kansalaisia syntymästään lähtien perustuslain 14. lisäyksen nojalla.

Trump oli pyrkinyt muuttamaan käytäntöä presidentin määräyksellä. Hänen tavoitteensa oli evätä automaattinen Yhdysvaltain kansalaisuus lapsilta, jotka syntyvät maassa vanhemmille, joilla ei ole pysyvää tai laillista asemaa. Korkein oikeus katsoi, ettei presidentti voi muuttaa kansalaisuuden määritelmää yksin toimeenpanomääräyksellä.

Päätös koskee pitkään voimassa ollutta tulkintaa, jonka mukaan Yhdysvaltain maaperällä syntynyt lapsi saa kansalaisuuden syntymän perusteella. Käytäntöä on lähteiden mukaan pidetty keskeisenä osana Yhdysvaltain perustuslaillista järjestelmää noin 150 vuoden ajan.

## Reaktiot korostavat perustuslain rajoja

Päätös herätti reaktioita eri puolilla maata. Oklahomassa poliittinen analyytikko Scott Mitchell kuvasi ratkaisua kysymykseksi vallan rajoista ja presidentin toimivallasta. Hänen mukaansa osavaltiot, jotka haastoivat Trumpin määräyksen, voittivat, koska korkein oikeus ei sallinut presidentin ohittaa perustuslakia.

Massachusettsin kuvernööri Maura Healey kiitti ratkaisua lausunnossaan. Hänen mukaansa päätös vahvistaa perustuslaillisen periaatteen, joka on määrittänyt Yhdysvaltoja sukupolvien ajan. Healey sanoi syntymäoikeuteen perustuvan kansalaisuuden tuoneen varmuutta perheille eri puolilla maata ja suojaavan Yhdysvaltain maaperällä syntyneiden lasten oikeuksia.

## Ratkaisun merkitys

Ratkaisua pidetään takaiskuna Trumpin maahanmuuttopolitiikalle. Se myös vahvistaa tuomioistuimen kannan, jonka mukaan presidentin toimeenpanovalta ei riitä muuttamaan perustuslaissa turvattua kansalaisuuden perustaa. BBC kertoi kysyneensä amerikkalaisilta, miten he suhtautuivat päätökseen, joka koskee Yhdysvalloissa syntyvien lasten kansalaisuutta.
